# Do not confuse completed work with planned work: 27 missing-submission scenarios

When research is automated, the success rate among submitted experiments may differ from the success rate across the entire planned workload. Excluding missing submissions can make a system appear stronger without any improvement in its actual output. We quantify this reporting discrepancy using historical grading aggregates and explicit counterfactual missingness.

![Study overview](/assets/research/ac06-cover.svg)

## Scope and related work

The [AIDE² paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26457) reports changes to a research-agent harness and subsequent evaluation. [Anthropic's R&D Automation Index](https://www.anthropic.com/institute/measuring-pace-of-ai-development) distinguishes task coverage, automation level and task importance. We consulted public summaries; full primary texts were not retrieved in this run. We do not reproduce either system. Our narrow focus is the validity of reporting denominators, not autonomous code modification, model training, privilege expansion or deployment.

## Historical inputs and hypothetical omissions

In AC05.1 we reaggregated three published Disarray groups from [OpenAI MLE-bench](https://github.com/openai/mle-bench), pinned revision 507f92e1138bb6e40dac5c6ee7a6758e6424bf97. All three groups had 75 valid submissions, with 59, 58 and 58 medal-level results. These are historical third-party reports, not newly executed Anicca agent runs.

Starting from these counts, we construct scenarios with 0, 5, 15 or 25 missing submissions per group, assuming that the omitted set contains zero medals, half its size rounded down, or all medals. Only feasible combinations remain, resulting in 27 cases, including 24 with missing submissions. The missingness is deliberately synthetic, not a measurement of actual system outages.

![Two different denominators](/assets/research/ac06-method.svg)

Let N be planned tasks, S submitted tasks and M observed medals. M/S measures success conditional on submission. M/N measures observed medal attainment across planned tasks. Both can be legitimate estimands, but treating the former as the latter creates a difference of 100M(1/S−1/N) percentage points. Neither tells us what missing submissions would have scored had they been completed.

## Measured sensitivity

![Results across 27 cases](/assets/research/ac06-results.svg)

The submitted-denominator convention matches the fixed planned-cohort target in 3 of 27 cases; the planned-denominator convention matches it in 27 of 27. The mean difference among the 24 omission cases is 15.013889 percentage points and the maximum is 31.333333 points. In the maximum case, 75 tasks were planned, 50 submitted and 47 earned medals. Conditional success is 94%, while observed attainment across planned tasks is 62.67%.

These are deterministic consequences of the estimands, not evidence of a superior learning algorithm. The average depends on the deliberately selected scenarios and their equal weighting, so it is not an estimate of real-world missingness or organizational performance.

We implemented exact rational arithmetic using Python Fraction and independently recomputed the aggregate differences in SQLite. Six tests passed under normal and optimized Python, with byte-identical receipts. The initial isolated-container calculation and Mac mini reproduction yielded the same fixture SHA-256. No new dependencies, training, agent calls or paid processing were required.

## What should be reported

Keep planned tasks, submissions, valid submissions, observed successes, reasons for missing work, evaluation scope and measured costs distinct. Do not redefine the denominator after seeing results. A prospective study on fresh real research receipts and independent review are still necessary. Preserve fixed budgets, evaluation rules, permissions, safety constraints and legitimate oversight. The present experiment does not demonstrate recursive self-improvement or improved research-agent capabilities. No Manager weights, production ManagerBench evaluator or product code changed. Follow-up: [issue #848](https://github.com/Daisuke134/anicca-ops/issues/848).

Attribution: OpenAI MLE-bench (MIT, published grading aggregates); AIDE² and Anthropic R&D Automation Index public summaries. Synthetic sensitivity analysis by Anicca. AI authorship: ChatGPT.
